note: Steady state, every router already knows its hop count to net N.
R1 forwards to R2, the only next hop R1 knows about.
R2 does the same with its own table. It has no memory of where the packet came from, and no idea where it's ultimately headed.
Delivered. Three independent lookups, no router ever saw the whole path.
R3's link to net N drops. R3 knows immediately.
R2's routine update still says 2, stale, from before the break. R3 trusts it: 2 + 1 = 3. A loop has formed: R3 now routes toward R2, and R2 still routes toward R3.
Converged, two floods, every router certain.
A real packet for net N arrives at R2 right now and gets caught in that loop.
TTL hit zero, discarded. The loop won't clear until the hop count climbs high enough to be declared infinite.
R2 hears R3's new number and adds one: 4.
R3 adds one again: 5, and this keeps going, every round, up toward 16.
Eventually the count reaches 16, RIP's definition of infinity. Only then do R2 and R3 agree net N is truly gone.
The news reaches R1 the same way every number here traveled, one hop at a time.
